sections.title: What a lesson plan is for

blocks.x: A lesson plan is a map for the lesson, not a script. It helps you decide what learners should achieve, what they will do to get there, and how you will know they have learned it.

items: You teach with a clear aim instead of filling time.
You think about problems before they happen.
You use time, materials and learner energy on purpose.
You can reflect afterwards and improve the next lesson.
A mentor, a substitute teacher or an inspector can see what you intended.
Learner-centred: it says what learners do, not only what you do.
Short and usable: one or two pages you can glance at while teaching.
Flexible: you can change it when learners need something different.
Realistic: the timing allows for instructions, feedback and moving between activities.

blocks.x: Plan for learning, not for teaching. If every stage describes only what the teacher says, the plan is incomplete.

sections.title: Pre-thinking: before you write the plan

blocks.x: Pre-thinking is the thinking you do before you write anything down. Work through these questions first. The answers make the written plan quick to write and sensible to teach.

Think about

Talk about future plans using going to
What do they need to know?
Language: meaning, form, pronunciation, use. Other subjects: key concepts, terms and steps
Meaning: a plan made before now. Form: be + going to + verb. Weak sound of to. Use: plans and predictions
Likely errors, confusing ideas, first-language influence, vocabulary, the wording of instructions
Forgetting be (I going to travel), pronunciation of going to
What came before, what comes next, the unit or syllabus
After the lesson on weekend vocabulary, before a unit review
How will I know they learned?
The evidence you will see or hear

Time, room, board, books, printouts, electricity, projector, helpers
45 minutes, board and textbook, no projector
Problems and a backup (see Anticipating problems and plan B)

items: Write the aim and the success criteria first.
Choose a procedure that fits the aim (see Procedures).
Then fill in the stage table, timing and materials.

blocks.x: These are the same sections as your planner form, so you can use this table as a checklist while you fill it in.
By the end of the lesson, students will be able to + verb + what + (how or how well)

head: Level of thinking
Useful verbs
rows: explain, describe, summarise, give an example

justify, give an opinion, choose and explain

head: Weak
Better
Why
rows: Students will understand the present perfect.

Understand cannot be seen. Writing sentences can be checked.
Teach students about the water cycle.

The weak version describes the teacher. The better version describes the learners.

items: Write one to three objectives. More than that is usually too much for one lesson.
Check that every stage helps reach at least one objective.
Add a success criterion in learner language: I can...

blocks.x: Most lessons have the same shape: get ready, learn something, practise it, use it, and finish. The names change between procedures, but the purposes stay the same.

head: Stage
Purpose
Teacher
Learners
About (45 min)
rows: Interest, context, activate what they know
Asks questions, shows a picture or starts a short game
Sets the context, models, explains, checks understanding
Gives exercises or drills, corrects quickly
Practise as a class, in pairs or alone
Sets a task with a purpose, monitors, notes errors
Use the language to complete the task
Shares good examples and common errors without naming learners
Summarises, asks an exit question, sets homework

items: Not every lesson needs every stage. Skills lessons often use pre-, while- and post- stages instead.
Write each stage's aim in a short phrase. If you cannot, the stage may not be needed.
Keep time for the wrap-up even when an earlier stage runs over.

blocks.x: Learners' energy rises and falls during a lesson. Stirrers raise it and settlers calm it. Planning both on purpose keeps attention high without losing control.

head: Stirrer
Settler
rows: Board race, running dictation, mingle, Simon says, team quiz, change partners, find someone who
Silent reading, individual writing, quiet puzzle or word search, copying from the board, drawing from a description, writing a reflection note
Learners are tired or bored, after long sitting or listening, at the start of a low-energy lesson, before a group task
After a game, before listening or a test, when the room is too noisy, before careful writing
Noise, lost time, weaker learners left out
A long settler makes learners drift, so keep it purposeful

items: Picture the lesson as a line that goes up and down. Mark where you want high energy and where you want calm.
Put a settler before work that needs concentration, and a stirrer when attention drops.
Avoid two stirrers in a row without a reason, and avoid a long unbroken settler with younger learners.
Link each one to the aim: a stirrer should still practise language or content.
Teach the routines first: a signal to stop, how to move, who does what in a group.
Keep movement small: stand up in teams, pass papers along rows, work with the nearest partner.
Give every learner a job, such as writer, reporter or timekeeper.

blocks.x: In your plan, write stirrer or settler beside the activity and note the interaction pattern. It shows you have balanced the lesson.

head: Pattern
Good for
Watch for
rows: Few learners speak, others switch off
Noise, one learner doing all the work
Projects, discussion, problem solving, role play
Off-task talk, unequal participation. Give roles.

items: Change the pattern when the activity changes. It also changes the energy.
Use pairs before groups, and groups before open discussion.
Pair stronger and weaker learners for support, or similar levels for challenge.
Give group roles: leader, writer, reporter, timekeeper.

blocks.x: A procedure is the order of stages you follow. Choose it by the aim and the learners, not by habit.

head: Procedure
Best for
Learners
Teacher control
Main idea
rows: New, clearly defined grammar or functions
The same, with support reduced step by step
Try the task, teach the gaps, try again
Engage, study, activate, in any order
Prepare, read or listen with tasks, respond
I do, We do, You do
Learners notice the rule from examples

blocks.x: No procedure is best. You can mix them. A PPP grammar stage can sit inside a PWP reading lesson.
The most widely taught sequence for new grammar and functional language. The teacher presents the language, learners practise it in a controlled way, then use it more freely.

head: Stage
Aim
Teacher
Learners
rows: Sets a context (story, picture, situation), elicits and models the language, checks meaning with concept questions, shows the form on the board
Gives drills, gap-fills, matching and short question and answer, corrects immediately
Practise as a class, in pairs and alone
Sets a communicative task (role play, information gap, discussion), monitors, notes errors
Use the language to complete the task

blocks.x: Example: going to for plans (45 min)

head: Stage
Activity
rows: Ask: What are you going to do this weekend? Take two or three answers.
Show a diary with pictures. Elicit: Sokha is going to visit his grandmother. Check meaning and form. Drill the sentences.
Substitution drill, then a gap-fill, then pair question and answer.
Pairs interview each other about next weekend, then report one fact to the class.
Correct common errors from the board. Learners write two sentences for homework.

items: The language item is new and clearly defined.
Learners are beginners or elementary, or the class is large.
You need a clear, controllable structure.
It is linear and assumes learners learn what you teach in that order.
Production can feel artificial and learners may not use the new language naturally.
It ignores what learners already know.
Present in a context, not in isolated sentences.
Check meaning before form.
Keep the presentation under ten minutes.
Move quickly from controlled practice to meaningful practice.
Give the production task a real purpose and save correction until afterwards.

sections.title: PRS: Presentation, Restricted practice, Structured production

blocks.x: PRS is often presented in teacher training as a variant of PPP. It has the same three-step shape, but it names the practice and production stages by how much freedom learners have: restricted, then structured, and finally free if time allows. This makes it easy to plan a gradual release of support.

head: Stage
Learner freedom
What happens
rows: Set the context, show the meaning, form and pronunciation, and check understanding, as in PPP.
Drills, substitution, matching, gap-fills and controlled dialogues. The focus is accuracy and immediate correction.
Learners produce the language using prompts, role cards, sentence frames or a guided dialogue. The target language is guided but the content is partly theirs.
An open task with no frame, such as a discussion or a group presentation, once learners are secure.

head: Stage
Activity
rows: Drill: I am going to play football. Change play football to swim, read, visit my aunt.
Dialogue frame in pairs: What are you going to do on ___? I am going to ___ because ___.
Groups plan a class picnic and present their plan to the class.

items: Learners need more support between a drill and free speaking or writing.
The class has mixed levels: stronger learners can drop the frame sooner.
You want to describe the middle of a PPP lesson more precisely.
Plan a ladder of freedom: drill, then prompts, then a frame, then an open task.
Prepare the prompts or frames before the lesson.
Remove the support in steps when learners succeed.
Terminology differs between courses. Follow your own course's wording in the written plan.

blocks.x: Learners try a task first, you teach only what they could not do, and then they try a similar task again. It starts from what learners already know.

head: Stage
Aim
What happens
rows: Learners attempt a task that needs the target language, with no teaching first. You monitor and note three to five important errors or gaps.
Teach only the language learners needed: meaning, form, pronunciation, with short practice.
Learners do a similar task. Compare with the first attempt.

items: It is revision, or learners already know part of the language.
Learners are intermediate or above, or the class is mixed.
You want to teach only what is needed.
It is less predictable and needs flexible, confident teaching.
Lower levels may struggle with the first task.
Choose a task that naturally needs the target language.
Write down the errors during the first task so you can teach from them.
Make the second task similar enough to compare.

head: Element
Aim
Examples
rows: Picture, game, story, music, surprising question
Focus on how language or content works
Use language as freely as possible
Role play, discussion, writing task, project

head: Pattern
Order
Use for
rows: Like TTT: try first, study the gaps, try again

blocks.x: An activate stage is not finished until learners have used the language. A study stage is not finished until they understand it.

sections.title: PWP: Pre, While, Post (reading and listening)

blocks.x: For skills lessons. Learners prepare for the text, work through it with tasks, and then respond to it.

head: Stage
Aim
Ideas
rows: Talk about the title or picture, predict, pre-teach only three to five essential words, set a purpose for reading or listening
First read or listen for gist (the general idea), then again for detail, with tasks such as true or false, matching, ordering, completing a table
Discuss opinions, role play, write a summary, link to their own lives, study useful phrases from the text

items: Set the task before learners read or listen, not after.
Give a different purpose each time: gist first, then detail.
Do not ask learners to understand every word.
Let learners check answers in pairs before the whole-class check.
Play audio two or three times at most, each time with a new task.

blocks.x: Learners do a meaningful task first, using whatever language they have. Language study comes after the task, based on what they needed.

head: Stage
What happens
rows: Introduce the topic and the task: brainstorm words, show a model of the task.
Pairs or groups do the task while you monitor. The focus is on getting the job done.
Learners prepare to report their results to the class.
Groups present or compare their results.
Analyse the language from the task and practise useful items, using errors you noted.

items: Learners are intermediate or above and fairly confident.
You want communication and fluency.
It needs more time and is harder to manage in very large classes.
Weaker learners need support with language during the task.

head: Stage
What happens
rows: Show a phenomenon, picture or question from daily life. Learners predict.
Learners investigate with a demonstration, experiment, source or diagram.
Learners and teacher explain the concept and the vocabulary.
Learners apply the idea to a new problem or situation.
Check understanding with questions, a short quiz or a task.

blocks.x: I do, We do, You do (gradual release)

items: I do: you model the skill or solve an example while thinking aloud.
We do: you and the learners do an example together; learners answer.
You do: learners practise alone or in pairs while you monitor and help.
Use it for maths, writing and any step-by-step skill.
Show examples of the language or pattern.
Ask learners to notice what is the same.
Guide them to state the rule in their own words.
Confirm the rule, then practise it.

blocks.x: Many subject lessons also use a simple five-part plan: warm-up and review, new content, guided practice, independent practice, wrap-up.

items: Plan each stage in minutes and add them up. Round to five minutes.
Leave a buffer of about five minutes for instructions and surprises.
Mark which parts you must do and which you could drop if time runs short.
Plan the move from one stage to the next: how you will stop, give instructions and regroup.
Move materials and furniture before the lesson, not during it.
Always keep the wrap-up, even if you must shorten a practice stage.

blocks.x: Most new teachers plan too much. If in doubt, plan one activity fewer.

items: Get everyone's attention.
Give the instruction in short steps, one at a time.
Demonstrate with an example or one learner.
Check understanding with instruction-checking questions (ICQs).
Start the activity and monitor.

head: Check
Examples
rows: Are you working alone or in pairs? How many sentences do you write? How much time do you have?
Did I do this in the past? (Yes) Do I do it now? (No)
Have I decided already? (Yes) Is it in the future? (Yes)

items: Elicit (draw out) answers from learners before you tell them.
Wait three to five seconds after a question before you choose someone.
Ask open questions as well as closed ones.
Do not ask Do you understand? Ask a question that shows it.

head: Problem
Possible solution
rows: Prepare an extension task, such as write more, make a new example, or help a partner
Learners do not understand the instructions
Demonstrate, shorten the instruction, check with ICQs
Agree a stop signal, use a settler, reduce the group size
A stage takes longer than planned
Use your could-drop list; shorten practice, never the wrap-up
Use support and extension tasks, mixed pairs, choice of task
Have the key content on the board or on a handout
Learners use their first language too much
Give a clear language goal, pre-teach phrases, praise use of the target language
Change the pattern, add a stirrer, connect to their lives
Use the board, learner-made materials, cut-up cards

blocks.x: Write the two or three most likely problems and your solutions in the plan. That is your plan B.

items: Give sentence frames, word banks or a worked example.
Pair a learner who needs help with a stronger partner.
Break a task into smaller steps with a quick check after each.
Add a challenge: more detail, a second example, or explaining to a partner.
Let fast finishers create questions for the class.
Use pair and group work with roles so everyone has a job.
Use choral repetition, then pairs, then a few individual answers.
Walk around in a pattern so you reach every group.
Use the board and written tasks that can be checked in pairs.
The aim is clear and measurable.
Every stage helps reach the aim.
The procedure suits the aim and the learners.
There is variety in interaction patterns and energy (stirrers and settlers).
The timing is realistic and includes a wrap-up.
I know how I will check understanding.
Instructions are short and I have planned the demonstration.
Materials are ready and I have a low-tech alternative.
I have support and extension tasks.
I have a plan B for the most likely problems.
I know what homework I will set and how I will explain it.

blocks.x: Reflect on the same day, while you still remember. Write short, honest notes. They are the start of your next plan.

items: What went well, and why?
What was difficult, and why?
Were the objectives achieved? What is the evidence?
Which learners needed more help or more challenge?
Was the timing right? What would I cut or add?
What will I change next time?
What should the next lesson cover?

blocks.x: Turn reflection into action: choose one thing to change in your next lesson and write it at the top of your next plan.
